U.S. stocks soared after President Donald Trump's party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.

Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6% Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 1,500 points, and the Nasdaq composite rose 1.4%.

Stocks of hospital owners and retailers focused on lower-income Americans led the widespread rally. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump's social-media company, the AI industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk. Oil prices tumbled, which helped Treasury yields to ease in the bond market.

On Wednesday:

The S&P 500 rose 119.70 points, or 1.6%, to 7,688.62.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,569.40 points, or 3%, to 53,356.12.

The Nasdaq composite rose 364.50 points, or 1.4%, to 25,736.51.

The Russell 2000 rose 44.50 points, or 1.6%, to 2,856.95.

title: Why D-Wave Quantum Stock Led a Quantum Computing Crash in October
detail:
Why D-Wave Quantum Stock Led a Quantum Computing Crash in October
Anders Bylund, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 2:07 PM MST 4 min read
QBTS
^GSPC
IONQ
RGTI
QNT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Shares of D-Wave Quantum (NASDAQ:QBTS) fell 35.7% in October 2026, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) barely noticed, slipping 0.9% over the same period. D-Wave didn't do anything wrong, exactly. It just happens to be in a sector that suddenly needed a lot of cash, and investors didn't love that idea.

A sectorwide retreat

D-Wave had plenty of quantum computing company on the way down. IonQ (NYSE:IONQ) fell 31.5% in October, Quantinuum (NASDAQ:QNT) dropped 30.1%, and Rigetti Computing (NASDAQ:RGTI) lost 28.5%. The four stocks moved in near lockstep for most of the month, and that's just the top of a long list. D-Wave plunged just a little faster than the rest.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The real trouble started with IonQ. First, it agreed to buy cybersecurity firm Elisity for $1.3 billion in stock. Then it announced a $2 billion equity offering. D-Wave's stock fell on both occasions. That's a lot of new shares hitting the market in a hurry, and it reminded everyone that many quantum computing companies are burning through lots of cash nowadays. Dilutive fundraising always lurks just around the corner. It was IonQ last month, and D-Wave could be next, even with a decent cash cushion.

Later in the month, Barron's published an article questioning when the industry's technical promises will translate into meaningful revenue. D-Wave's annealing technology sets it apart from the competition for now, but rivals could enter this sub-market over time. And neither annealing computers nor quantum gate systems are powerful enough to solve the digital world's impossible problems at this point.

D-Wave's own news was pretty good. It extended a manufacturing deal with IonQ's SkyWater Technology, shipped Italy's first annealing quantum computer, and signed a partnership with LG CNS in South Korea. But none of these helpful events could stop D-Wave's slide.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Big promises, small revenue

Let's talk valuation. D-Wave brought in $12.4 million of revenue over the last four quarters, down 44.2% year over year. The stock is still worth about $3.9 billion. That's roughly 316 times sales, a multiple that assumes a lot of growth is right around the corner.

In all fairness, D-Wave won't run out of money in 2027. The company holds roughly $500 million in net cash and carries little debt, so it is not under immediate pressure to raise funds. Short-sellers have bet against about 21.6% of the stock's float, however, and that kind of bearish pressure tends to amplify price swings in both directions.

title: If the S&P 500 Falls 20%, Here's the 1 ETF I'd Buy Hand Over Fist
detail:
If the S&P 500 Falls 20%, Here's the 1 ETF I'd Buy Hand Over Fist
Ben Gran, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 1:20 PM MST 4 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase

There's no such thing as a "perfect" investment strategy or a "can't miss" investment. Every stock and sector of the economy can be risky. Even the S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) of the largest 500 publicly traded companies in America can have a bad day, year, or decade.

Currently, lots of investors are worried about a possible stock market crash. The past few years of investor excitement about artificial intelligence (AI) stocks are hitting some fresh doubts and skepticism. In the past few weeks since reaching a new record high on Oct. 6, the S&P 500 has declined by about 3% as of this writing.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What if the S&P 500 drops by another 17%? What if the S&P 500 goes into a bear market, with a 20% decline?

It's easier to say than to do, but the truth is: If the S&P 500 falls 20%, I would buy more of the S&P 500. The Vanguard S&P 500 exchange-traded fund (ETF) (NYSEMKT: VOO) is one of the best ways to own these 500 companies for long-term investors.

Image source: Getty Images.
Why buy VOO if the stock market crashes?

The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF lets you own a diversified portfolio of 505 stocks, representing all 500 of the largest publicly traded companies in America. This includes major AI stocks like Nvidia and Alphabet, as well as large financial services companies like JPMorgan Chase and healthcare companies like Eli Lilly.

No one knows which of America's largest companies will deliver the best profits and biggest shareholder returns in the future. Even if the AI stock market boom turns into an AI crash, the overall S&P 500 index might do better than the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100. That's exactly what happened in 2022 during the most recent bear market:

^NDX data by YCharts.

None of this means that the S&P 500 or VOO are "safe" investments. They can lose value. They can go through a crash or a longer-term bear market. But most of the time, even with big crashes in the short run, the S&P 500 and VOO are great investments. Here's why.

The S&P 500 has 98 years of 9.98% annualized returns

Let's go back in time to 1928. The Roaring Twenties. Investors had survived a terrible pandemic and were excited about new technologies like the radio and the automobile. People thought this transformational technology-driven economic boom would keep going forever.

Then in 1929, it all crashed. The Great Depression happened next. Then World War II. Think of all the terrible tragedies and economic challenges America has faced since 1928.

title: Can Lockheed Martin Stock Compound Your Money?
detail:
Can Lockheed Martin Stock Compound Your Money?
Trefis Team

LMT
^GSPC
NOC
RTX
BA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Shares of Lockheed Martin (LMT) returned 33.3% over the year to November 3, 2026, outpacing the 11.9% return for the S&P 500. The company continually repurchases its own stock, reducing its diluted share count by 7.5% over the three years to September 2026, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice of the business. How much has that smaller share count added to what each share earns?

Each Lockheed Martin Share Earns More Despite Lower Profit

Lockheed Martin's earnings per share grew 0.94% a year over the three years to September 2026, even as its net income fell 2.2% a year. The smaller share count explains most of that annual difference of about 3.2 percentage points.

The pace of those repurchases has slowed every year. After falling 5.6% in the twelve months to September 2023, the share count declined by 4.6% in the following twelve months. It then dropped 2.4%, and fell only 0.56% in the twelve months to September 2026. Lockheed spent $0.75 billion on buybacks during that latest stretch, compared with $7.21 billion in the twelve months to September 2023. Net buying amounted to just 0.27% of the company's market value after accounting for what it spent on stock pay for employees.

Lockheed Earns Twice As Much Cash As It Returns

Surplus cash funds Lockheed Martin's buybacks and dividends. The company generated $8.38 billion in free cash flow over the twelve months to September 2026, or 2.1 times the $3.96 billion returned to shareholders. Based on the November 3 close, that free cash flow equated to about $57 a year for every $1,000 of stock.

A growing business generates this cash. Revenue climbed 7.9% to $79.1 billion over those twelve months, and the operating margin reached 11.8%, compared with 8.3% a year earlier. Management said third-quarter sales rose in every segment, including F-35 production, and the company ended September with a record backlog of $292 billion.

Dividends now make up most of what Lockheed hands back to investors. The company paid out $3.21 billion over the twelve months, more than four times its buyback spending. The board raised the quarterly dividend to $3.60 a share in October, marking the company's 24th consecutive year of dividend increases.

Lockheed Martin Has Other Calls On Its Cash

Lockheed Martin carries moderate debt relative to its earnings. Net debt stood at $14.5 billion at the end of September 2026, representing about 1.4 times a year's EBITDA, its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Operating profit covered the interest bill 8.6 times over the past twelve months.

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stock Preachers News Commentary - The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,572.58 points, or 3.04%, at 53,359.30 as of 2:45 p.m. ET on Wednesday, putting it back above its 50-day moving average. The S&P 500 was up 1.78% and the Nasdaq Composite was up 1.83% at the same time, and all four major U.S. indexes were trading higher. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: 3M Company (NYSE: MMM), Stanley Black & Decker, Inc. (NYSE: SWK), CDW Corporation (Nasdaq: CDW), Booking Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ: BKNG), Duolingo, Inc. (NASDAQ: DUOL).

Stock Preachers Logo

Big up days tend to get summed up with one number. But the more useful story for chart readers is where prices landed relative to the levels traders watch.

Wednesday's session follows Tuesday's U.S. elections. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, according to race calls by The Associated Press as of 2:57 a.m. ET Wednesday.

Charts don't take sides, though. They simply record where buyers and sellers agreed on a price, and on Wednesday they recorded a lot of agreement at higher levels.

Can you read a chart when the whole market moves at once?

Our free 27-page guide, Knowledge is Power, walks through support, resistance, trendlines and the indicators that matter, in plain English. Get the free guide at stockpreachers.com »

The Dow and the S&P 500 are back above a line many chartists watch

The 50-day simple moving average is the average of the last 50 daily closes. Many technical traders watch it as a rough gauge of the intermediate trend.

Based on daily closing prices through Tuesday, the Dow's 50-day average stood at 52,152.95, and the S&P 500's at 7,692.74. Both indexes had closed below those levels on Oct. 30, Nov. 2 and Nov. 3. As of 2:45 p.m. ET, the S&P 500 was at 7,703.81, up 134.89 points, just above that line.

The picture was less tidy elsewhere. The Nasdaq Composite was at 25,837.47, still below its 50-day average of 26,541.66, a level it hasn't closed above since Oct. 21. The Russell 2000 was up 1.45% at 2,853.10 at the same time, a hair above its 50-day average of 2,851.68.

Here's the thing: the bigger chart moves on Wednesday came from individual stocks with fresh company news. Each of the five below opened above its prior session's high, leaving a price gap that, as of the same time stamp, had not been filled.

Three stocks gapped up to fresh 52-week highs

3M Company (NYSE: MMM) said on Nov. 3 that it entered into a broad resolution to settle PFAS-related personal injury claims that are the focus of the Aqueous Film-Forming Foam Multi-District Litigation. Under the agreement, 3M will make a pre-tax $7.35 billion nominal commitment over nine years, with a present value of $5.8 billion, and the company said the resulting charge does not change its previously issued 2026 guidance.

title: Democrats' Resounding Win in the Midterms Removed Political Uncertainty. Stocks Soared.
detail:
Democrats' Resounding Win in the Midterms Removed Political Uncertainty. Stocks Soared.
Demian Bio
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 2:03 PM MST 2 min read
CL=F
^DJI
^GSPC
^IXIC

Stocks soared on Wednesday, with the Dow Jones closing its best day in a year and a half after the decisive win by the Democratic party removed some political uncertainty in the U.S.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite gained 1.44%, while the S&P 500 did so 1.58%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average overperformed, soaring 3.03%.

President Donald Trump quickly accepted the result, saying he would be willing to work with Democrats over the next two years. The party will now control both chambers of Congress after seeing historical gains, including in Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.

Oil prices also plunged after the GOP's rout in the midterms and the acknowledgment by top Republicans that the Iran war played a key role in it.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell more than 8% and stood just above $95 a barrel at 3:28 p.m. ET, while West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, plummeted 7.77% and stood at $88.62 per barrel at the same time.

Vice President JD Vance blamed the war for the results in a lengthy social media publication, claiming that an "honest conversation" needs to be had about it moving forward.

"Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026," Vance said in a passage of the post.

He went on to concede the argument from a pollster who told him the administration's economic message "wasn't sharp enough down the stretch," but the "real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone."

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there," Vance added.

He concluded by saying that he is "hopeful" about the future of the U.S., calling on people who "want to say 'I told you so'" to do it but help elect "Republicans who share your worldview.

Trump also acknowledged that the Iran war, which contributed to soaring gas prices in the U.S. and around the world, played a role in the results, but said he doesn't regret his decision.

"Iran was a piece of it," the president told The Wall Street Journal as the results came in. "I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he added.

Trump went on to note that rising gas prices, rather than the war itself, turned voters against the Republican party.
